What Survives When You Compress a Recursive Reasoner for the Edge?

Pearse Jim ††thanks:   Equal Contribution. Affiliation: ML Collective    Steven Kolawole11footnotemark: 1 Affiliation: ML Collective Affiliation: Carnegie Mellon University    Opegbemi M. Busoye Affiliation: ML Collective    Glory Bagai Affiliation: ML Collective    Virginia Smith Affiliation: Carnegie Mellon University
Abstract

Recursive reasoning models solve hard structured tasks with a few million parameters by iterating a latent state, but deploying them on edge hardware means compressing them – and quantization noise compounds across recursive cycles rather than accumulating over output tokens, so single-pass intuitions fail. Here, we ask what survives. Across a full precision sweep and three tasks, aggressive compression preserves local prediction but destroys global reasoning: pruning, distillation, and linear attention drive puzzle-exact accuracy to zero while cell accuracy holds. Naïve INT4 is different: its damage is architectural, striking MLP-mixing recursion but not attention on the same task, and per-channel calibration reverses it without retraining, where quantization-aware training does not. We also introduce carry-trajectory fidelity, the cosine similarity to the full-precision reasoning path, as a label-free signal that predicts both the damage and the recovery before any task evaluation, with a threshold that transfers across tasks. The result is a deployment recipe: flash-streamed embeddings remove a 99.4 MB bottleneck, one recursive cycle matches full-depth accuracy at 6×6\times fewer FLOPs, and calibrated INT4 brings the backbone to 3.3 MB, inside a 4 MB budget.

1 Introduction

The Tiny Recursive Model (TRM) solves abstract reasoning puzzles with only 6.83M parameters (Jolicoeur-Martineau, 2025)—44.6% on ARC-AGI-1 with 1000-augmentation test-time voting (36.00% single-pass in our harness)—competitive with larger autoregressive systems on a benchmark designed to resist pattern matching (Chollet, 2019). It does so by iterating a latent carry state across recursive cycles, a mechanism shared by Universal Transformers (Dehghani et al., 2019) and depth-recurrent language models (Geiping et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025; Hao et al., 2025; Kohli et al., 2026). Yet TRM weighs ∼\sim126 MB, more than an order of magnitude beyond the kB-to-MB SRAM of the microcontroller tier we target. Deployment there requires compression. When such a model is squeezed, what survives and what breaks?

While single-pass transformer quantization is well-studied (noise accumulates over output tokens, and INT8 deployment is standard) (Nagel et al., 2021; Dettmers et al., 2022; Han et al., 2016), recursive models introduce a different failure mode: quantization noise compounds across HH recursive cycles at each carry-state update. Whether this compounding degrades reasoning has not been studied. While quantization harms single-pass reasoning chains (Li et al., 2025) and emergent abilities collapse below 4-bit (Liu et al., 2024), depth and precision are independent in those systems. In recursive models, they are not: the optimal operating point depends jointly on bit-width and depth.

We present the first systematic compression study of a recursive reasoning model under hard SRAM constraints (Lin et al., 2020; Abushahla et al., 2025). We sweep precision (FP32, FP16, INT8, INT4) and depth across three tasks (ARC-AGI-1, Maze-Hard, Sudoku-Extreme) and two architectures (TRM and HRM). As shown in Figure 1, the dominant memory bottleneck is the 99.4 MB puzzle embedding table, which we resolve via 2 KB flash loading, isolating backbone compression. Our primary contributions are:

  1. 1.

    We establish a depth–precision crossover with two separable effects: a single recursive cycle matches full-depth accuracy at 6×6\times fewer FLOPs—a depth effect (FP32 at H=1H{=}1 scores 35.75% vs. INT8’s 35.25%)—while INT8 adds a 4×4\times weight-memory reduction at no accuracy cost, an interaction absent from single-pass quantization (§4.2).

  2. 2.

    We identify a compositional collapse: under pruning, distillation, and linear-attention substitution, local token accuracy survives while global puzzle accuracy falls to zero; naïve INT4’s harm is architecture-dependent, and an attention-vs-MLP-mixing ablation shows the fragility is architectural, not task-intrinsic (§4.3).

  3. 3.

    We introduce carry-trajectory fidelity, a label-free detector that grades this damage and predicts its recovery from the model’s own hidden states, with no task labels (§4.5).

  4. 4.

    We derive and benchmark a deployment recipe: per-channel calibrated INT4 weights reach 3.26 MB, within a 4 MB microcontroller budget, with latency, memory, and file size measured directly on three Snapdragon mobile platforms (§4.4, 4.7).

2 Related Work

Overthinking in recursive models is named but not detectable.

Recurrent and weight-tied architectures are a parameter-efficient path to algorithmic reasoning (Dehghani et al., 2019), and recent depth-recurrent language models show iterative latent refinement scales favorably (Geiping et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025; Hao et al., 2025; Kohli et al., 2026). Bansal et al. (2022) name their central failure—overthinking, where too many iterations corrupt the instance—but detect it only by full task evaluation; Du et al. (2026) and Lu et al. (2025) find correctness signals in latent trajectories, yet none give a signal usable during inference without labels. Our carry-trajectory fidelity, grounded in Jiang et al. (2025)’s link between hidden-state cosine similarity and representational saturation, predicts collapse under quantization with no task evaluation.

Quantization-as-regularization has an uncharacterized depth dimension.

Quantization noise can act as a regulariser – pushing toward flatter minima with a model-specific optimal level (AskariHemmat et al., 2024; AskariHemmat et al., 2022), robust under distribution shift and limited data (Javed et al., 2025; Tallec et al., 2023), sometimes letting INT8 beat FP32 (Zhang et al., 2025) – which explains INT8 parity in single-pass models. None predicts recursive behavior, where the same noise is applied across HH carry-state updates and beneficial regularization at shallow depth becomes destructive compounding at depth. We characterize this depth–precision interaction directly.

Compressed reasoning fails early; low-bit recovery needs the right recipe.

On reasoning chains, PTQ induces early failures that cascade (Li et al., 2025), with a precision floor near 4-bit (Liu et al., 2024) and W8A8 as the lossless threshold for small models (Liu et al., 2025); consistent with our INT8 finding, but for single-pass decoding. Standard QAT recipes for reasoning models favor distillation/KD objectives and PTQ initialization (Lv et al., 2026); our QAT comparison follows that recipe (calibrated initialization, CE and KD objectives, three learning rates) and finds that further token-level training degrades an already-calibrated model (§4.6), so the quantizer is the reliable recovery path in our setting.

Edge NLP deployment motivates but does not resolve these questions.

Foundational compression (Han et al., 2016), the finding that pruning degrades small LMs more than quantization (Zhou et al., 2025) (consistent with our pruning results), INT8 as the deployment-native format (Dettmers et al., 2022; Kim et al., 2021), sub-megabyte MCU inference via hardware co-design (Lin et al., 2020), MCU-quantization surveys at our 4–8 MB constraints (Abushahla et al., 2025), and on-device NLP pipelines (Bohdal et al., 2025): none studies recursive reasoning models or the depth–precision interplay. No prior work compresses a recursive reasoning model; the closest (Li et al., 2025) addresses single-pass decoding and lacks the recursive carry-state structure we study.

3 Background and Experimental Setup

3.1 Tiny Recursive Model (TRM)

TRM (Jolicoeur-Martineau, 2025) is a weight-tied recursive transformer that solves structured reasoning tasks through iterative latent refinement rather than autoregressive generation. Let 𝒱\mathcal{V} be a finite vocabulary and X∈𝒱TxX\in\mathcal{V}^{T_{x}} be an input sequence. TRM maintains a latent carry state updated across two nested loops.

Given an initial answer embedding Y0∈ℝTy×dY_{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{T_{y}\times d}, the model maintains a carry state Zh∈ℝTz×dZ_{h}\in\mathbb{R}^{T_{z}\times d} across outer cycles h∈{1,…,H}h\in\{1,\dots,H\}. At each outer cycle, an inner loop executes LL refinement steps. A shared two-layer transformer block fθf_{\theta} updates the state:

Zh(l)=fθ​([X;Yh−1;Zh(l−1)])Z_{h}^{(l)}=f_{\theta}\!\left([X\,;\,Y_{h-1}\,;\,Z_{h}^{(l-1)}]\right) (1)

where [⋅;⋅][\cdot;\cdot] denotes sequence concatenation. After LL inner steps, the outer loop advances via:

Yh,Zh+1(0)=gϕ​(Zh(L))Y_{h},\;Z_{h+1}^{(0)}=g_{\phi}\!\left(Z_{h}^{(L)}\right) (2)

A one-step gradient approximation during training keeps memory 𝒪⁡(1)\mathcal{O}(1) with respect to recursive depth. The total number of refinement steps is H×nsupH\times n_{\text{sup}}, where nsupn_{\text{sup}} is the number of outer-loop supervision steps. At the default ARC-AGI-1 configuration (H=3H=3, nsup=16n_{\text{sup}}=16), TRM executes 48 refinement steps, incurring ∼\sim3,000 GFLOPs per puzzle over a 900-token sequence (𝒪⁡(n2)\mathcal{O}(n^{2}) attention).

We study two architectural variants: TRM-Attention, which uses multi-head self-attention over the full token sequence, and TRM-MLP-Mixing, which replaces attention with token-mixing MLP layers. These variants differ in how relational structure is encoded across refinement steps, which has consequences for compression sensitivity (§4.3).

3.2 Tasks and Datasets

ARC-AGI-1.

Abstract visual reasoning requiring detection of transformation rules across grid inputs (Chollet, 2019). We evaluate on the ARC-AGI-1 public evaluation set (400 tasks). TRM uses TRM-Attention with a 50,911-entry puzzle embedding table (99.4 MB in FP32) that provides puzzle-specific context and, in its published protocol, test-time augmentation (1,000 augmentations per puzzle) with multi-pass majority voting; our evaluations run single-pass (no TTA) unless noted. Parameters: 6.83M.

Maze-Hard.

Path-finding requiring exact end-to-end traversal over topological maps. Uses TRM-Attention without an embedding table or TTA. Parameters: 6.82M.

Sudoku-Extreme.

Constraint satisfaction over 9×99\times 9 grids with hard row, column, and block exclusions. Uses TRM-MLP-Mixing without an embedding table. Parameters: 5.03M.

We report two metrics throughout. Cell accuracy is the fraction of correct grid cells predictions. Puzzle exact match is the fraction of puzzles solved with zero errors. These metrics can diverge substantially: a model may predict nearly correct tokens (high cell accuracy) while satisfying zero global constraints (zero puzzle exact), as observed under several compression interventions (§4.6).

3.3 Evaluation Protocol

Headline evaluations use TRM’s test-time default: nsup=16n_{\text{sup}}{=}16, an fp32 forward pass, and random test subsets (Table 1). We call this the primary protocol. The wider sweeps and ablations, marked at point of use, run a lighter secondary protocol (nsup=10n_{\text{sup}}{=}10, bf16 forward, first-NN subsets) whose absolute accuracies sit a few points lower. The two protocols agree on every ordering this paper reports.

At this protocol naïve INT4 costs MLP-mixing 68.2 pp against 4.8 pp for attention on the same subset (Table 1).

3.4 Deployment Targets

The compression goal is on-device inference with no cloud dependency under hard SRAM constraints. Our target is the microcontroller tier: kB-to-MB SRAM, no DRAM, Cortex-M class, where the deployed state of the art is 1–2 MB CNNs (Lin et al., 2020) and nothing reasoning-capable is deployed at all. We use two budgets as reference points on the way there, 8 MB (mobile SoC SRAM, e.g. Cortex-A55) and 4 MB (MCU, e.g. Cortex-M55); the FP32 baseline (∼\sim126 MB total: 26.7 MB backbone + 99.4 MB embeddings) exceeds both by an order of magnitude.

Measurement cannot reach the target tier directly: no MCU toolchain runs these graphs today, so the on-device latency, memory, and model sizes of §4.7 come from three Snapdragon platforms via Qualcomm AI Hub (App. B), which are mobile-class. Everything we report at the 4 MB budget is therefore an analytical, weights-only projection (Table 4).

3.5 Compression Methods

Post-training quantization (PTQ).

We apply PTQ directly to the pretrained FP32 checkpoint, without retraining. FP16 halves memory via standard half-precision casting. INT8 uses per-channel scale calibration via bitsandbytes (Dettmers et al., 2022) - the standard format for hardware with integer acceleration units. INT4 naïve applies per-tensor PTQ without calibration. INT4 calibrated applies per-channel asymmetric PTQ (min/max range per output channel), again with no fine-tuning; it recovers most of the accuracy that naïve INT4 destroys (§4.4).

Structured pruning and knowledge distillation were also evaluated. Both collapse puzzle-level accuracy across all tasks while partially preserving cell accuracy (§4.6). We read this as a consequence of the model’s compactness: at 5–7M parameters there is too little redundancy to absorb pruning, and a single-pass student cannot capture the recursive computation.

Embedding compression.

For ARC-AGI-1, we separately evaluate three strategies for the 99.4 MB puzzle embedding table: INT8 quantization of the full table, SVD rank-16 factorization, and single-puzzle flash loading (streaming only the 2 KB row for the current puzzle at inference time).

3.6 Cycle Reduction

HH (outer cycles) and nsupn_{\text{sup}} (the number of outer-loop supervision steps) together determine total recursion depth: H=3H=3, nsup=16n_{\text{sup}}=16 means 48 sequential refinement steps on ARC-AGI-1. We sweep (H,nsup)∈{(1,1​–​16),(3,1​–​16)}(H,n_{\text{sup}})\in\{(1,1\text{--}16),\,(3,1\text{--}16)\} for ARC-AGI-1, and (H,nsup)∈{(1​–​4,1​–​10)}(H,n_{\text{sup}})\in\{(1\text{--}4,1\text{--}10)\} for Maze-Hard and Sudoku-Extreme. FLOPs scale linearly with total steps: at H=1H=1, nsup=8n_{\text{sup}}=8, the per-puzzle cost falls from ∼\sim3,000 GFLOPs to ∼\sim500 GFLOPs on ARC-AGI-1.

3.7 Carry-State Diagnostics

We use the recursive carry state to build a label-free signal for reasoning collapse under compression. Let Zh∈ℝTz×dZ_{h}\in\mathbb{R}^{T_{z}\times d} be the carry state after recursive call hh, with zh,iz_{h,i} its ii-th token vector.

Consecutive similarity (baseline).

The cosine similarity between successive carry states,

sh=1Tz​∑i=1Tzzh,i⋅zh−1,i‖zh,i‖2​‖zh−1,i‖2,s_{h}=\frac{1}{T_{z}}\sum_{i=1}^{T_{z}}\frac{z_{h,i}\cdot z_{h-1,i}}{\|z_{h,i}\|_{2}\,\|z_{h-1,i}\|_{2}}, (3)

measures per-step refinement (low shs_{h}) versus convergence to a near-fixed point (high shs_{h}), following Jiang et al. (2025)’s finding that hidden-state cosine similarity tracks representational saturation. We find this signal is nearly invariant to precision (§4.5) and thus a poor failure detector.

Carry-trajectory fidelity (primary).

The signal we recommend compares the compressed trajectory to the full-precision one. Let ZHqZ_{H}^{q} and ZHfp32Z_{H}^{\text{fp32}} be the final carry states of the quantized and FP32 models on the same input. Fidelity is

ϕ=1Tz​∑i=1TzzH,iq⋅zH,ifp32‖zH,iq‖2​‖zH,ifp32‖2.\phi=\frac{1}{T_{z}}\sum_{i=1}^{T_{z}}\frac{z_{H,i}^{q}\cdot z_{H,i}^{\text{fp32}}}{\|z_{H,i}^{q}\|_{2}\,\|z_{H,i}^{\text{fp32}}\|_{2}}. (4)

ϕ\phi quantifies how far quantization pushes the reasoning trajectory off the full-precision path. It requires only the FP32 reference (available before deployment) and no task labels, and—unlike shs_{h}—is graded and monotonic with the eventual accuracy loss (§4.5).

3.8 Quantization-Aware Training and Recovery

As a probe of whether a token-level objective can repair compression-induced reasoning loss, we run QAT from the calibrated-INT4 checkpoint: 1,000 steps at batch 32, under cross-entropy and token-distillation objectives at three learning rates each, with the deep-supervision ACT loop (§4.6). As the alternative recovery path we apply per-channel calibrated INT4 (a post-training quantizer with no fine-tuning) and report both its accuracy and its carry-trajectory fidelity (§4.4).

4 Results

4.1 The Embedding Table Dominates the Memory Footprint

The ARC-AGI-1 puzzle embedding table occupies 99.4 MB of the ∼\sim126 MB FP32 footprint, against 26.7 MB for the transformer backbone (Table 2). Three strategies were evaluated for embedding compression.

Only flash loading fits the deployment targets while preserving accuracy (Table 2): the 2 KB row for the current puzzle is streamed from flash at inference time, decoupling the embedding from the backbone compression problem. Figure 1 visualizes the resulting footprints. With the embedding handled, the backbone remains, and with it two levers: precision and recursion depth.

4.2 INT8 with Reduced Recursion Matches Full-Depth FP32

INT8 is lossless across both architectural variants and all three tasks (Table 8, Appendix C): per-channel calibration holds quantization error within what the recursive refinement process tolerates. The key efficiency gain therefore comes from cycle reduction, not precision: FP32 at H=1H{=}1, nsup=8n_{\text{sup}}{=}8 already scores 35.75% (Table 9), and INT8 at the same depth achieves 35.25% puzzle exact on ARC-AGI-1, single-pass (no test-time augmentation),11 1 All reported ARC accuracies are single-pass: the evaluation’s fast mode discarded the augmentations, so no augment-and-vote protocol was applied. TRM’s published 44.6% uses 1000-augmentation TTA and is not directly comparable. App. B compares the notebook harness with on-device execution. within 0.75 pp of the 36.00% full-depth baseline at 6×6\times fewer FLOPs (Figure 2). The two effects are separable: depth reduction supplies the 6×6\times FLOPs saving, while INT8 supplies a 4×4\times weight-memory reduction at no accuracy cost.

Across the full depth sweep (Appendices E and D), H=1H{=}1 brackets the 36.00% baseline from 34.25% (nsup=4n_{\text{sup}}{=}4) to 36.25% (nsup=16n_{\text{sup}}{=}16). The reduction holds on Maze-Hard (INT8 at H=1H{=}1, nsup=8n_{\text{sup}}{=}8 stays within 0.10 pp at 3.75×3.75\times fewer FLOPs). Sudoku-Extreme is the exception: its accuracy keeps climbing with depth within the swept range (best at H=4H{=}4, nsup≤10n_{\text{sup}}{\leq}10) and INT8 stays lossless there, so its full recursion cannot be cheaply cut (Appendices F, G).

Dynamic quantization preserves full-precision accuracy on every task, but NPU accelerators require static, pre-allocated tensor boundaries; the static path’s task-dependent penalties, and the operator exclusions Sudoku requires, are in Appendix B.2. INT8, then, is safe everywhere. INT4 is not, and where it breaks turns out to be the more informative finding.

4.3 Compression Fragility Is Architectural, Not Task-Intrinsic

The INT4 damage follows the architecture, not the task: the TRM-Attention tasks (ARC, Maze) tolerate naïve INT4 while TRM-MLP-Mixing (Sudoku) collapses (Table 8). This looks like a task-precision effect; a same-task ablation shows it is not (Figure 3; full grid in Appendix H).

Under naïve INT4, Maze-Hard loses 0.8 pp and ARC-AGI-1 loses 10.1 pp puzzle exact while keeping 89.2% cell accuracy, but Sudoku-Extreme collapses by 68.2 pp (primary protocol, Table 1; the official-checkpoint ARC figures are in §4.4). Since Sudoku was tested only with MLP-mixing, we re-run it with attention: TRM-Attention, at nearly the same full-precision accuracy on the same subset (73.1% vs. 74.6%), retains 68.3% under naïve INT4, and HRM (Wang et al., 2025) is also robust, while only MLP-mixing collapses (Table 15). The accuracy match rules out a headroom confound, locating the fragility in the token mixer. HRM, evaluated only on Sudoku and at a lower FP32 baseline, corroborates the pattern in a second model family rather than serving as a controlled comparison.

A weight-level mechanism.

Per-output-channel dynamic range explains why the token mixer specifically. On the two Sudoku checkpoints the token-mixing projections reach a 20.7×\times inter-channel spread, against 11.1×\times for the worst attention projection. Figure 4 shows the underlying distributions and extends the comparison to the deployment models: within the same network the token mixer’s spread is nearly three times the channel MLP’s, and both attention models sit lower still. The token mixer is the outlier on every comparison available to us, within a network and across them. Under a single per-tensor INT4 scale, the widest-spread channels dominate the quantization grid and narrow channels collapse into one or two bins. Per-channel calibration repairs exactly this, and the recovery of §4.4 follows. A failure rooted in per-channel spread implies a per-channel fix, which the next section tests.

4.4 Calibrated INT4 Recovers Constraint Reasoning

The catastrophic Sudoku-INT4 result is specific to naïve per-tensor quantization. Replacing it with per-channel calibrated INT4 (still 4-bit weights, still post-training, no fine-tuning) recovers essentially all of the lost accuracy: at the primary protocol, naïve INT4 drops Sudoku to 6.4% puzzle exact while calibrated INT4 reaches 74.5%, within 0.1 pp of the 74.6% FP32 baseline on the same subset (Table 1; secondary-protocol figures in App. I). The carry-trajectory fidelity diagnostic tracks this recovery with no task evaluation: fidelity rises from 0.350.35 (naïve, broken) to 0.890.89 (calibrated, recovered).

Measured on the official ARC checkpoint.

The same recovery holds on ARC-AGI-1, measured on the official TRM checkpoint (arcprize verification release; embedding table verified against the rebuilt official dataset, 876,406 identifiers), single-pass over all 400 evaluation tasks:

Calibration recovers ARC to within 0.1 pp of FP32 on a checkpoint anyone can download, and the fidelity column doubles as the held-out threshold test cited in §4.5.

This reframes the deployment floor: for constraint-satisfaction reasoning it is not INT8 but calibrated INT4, provided the quantizer is per-channel. Naïve INT4 remains unusable, and the diagnostic distinguishes the two before deployment.

4.5 Carry-Trajectory Fidelity Predicts Collapse and Recovery

The damage in §4.3 and its repair in §4.4 were both established by running the task. We now ask whether either can be predicted without doing so: a label-free signal that, before any task evaluation, tells whether a compression preserves or destroys reasoning. The obvious candidate (cosine similarity between consecutive carry states) does not work: it is task-specific but nearly invariant to precision, changing by ≤0.064\leq 0.064 from FP32 to INT4 on every task (App. I), so it cannot separate harmless from harmful compression.

The signal that does work is carry-trajectory fidelity: the cosine similarity between the quantized model’s final carry state and the full-precision model’s final carry state on the same input (§3.7). It measures how far quantization pushes the reasoning trajectory off the full-precision path, requires only the FP32 reference (available before deployment), and uses no task labels. Fidelity is graded and monotonic with damage (Figure 5; full data Appendix I): it stays ≥0.99\geq 0.99 wherever INT4 is harmless (Maze, and INT8 on every task) and falls in proportion to the accuracy loss, moderately on ARC and catastrophically on the Sudoku collapse of §4.3 (Table 17). It tracks the calibrated-INT4 recovery of §4.4 in the same way, rising as accuracy returns.

The threshold transfers across tasks.

We validate fidelity as a predictor on a 50-configuration grid spanning bit-widths, quantizer granularities and partial-layer sweeps across three model–task pairs (Appendix I); 8 configurations break, defined as a >>10 pp puzzle-exact drop. Spearman ρ\rho between fidelity and accuracy damage is −0.75-0.75 overall, fidelity separates broken from surviving configurations without error on this grid (AUC 1.00), and the dose–response is monotone (Figure 5). The threshold question now has a held-out answer: calibrated on Sudoku alone (τ=0.83\tau=0.83), it transfers to Maze without error. The official ARC checkpoint of §4.4 is a third, fully held-out test, on which the threshold was never calibrated: it flags naïve INT4 and clears calibrated INT4 (fidelity column of Table 3). An L2 trajectory-divergence baseline computed from the same captures is equally predictive on this grid; fidelity’s advantage is being bounded and scale-free across models, not higher discrimination. Quantization damage is therefore both repairable and predictable in advance. Neither holds for the remaining compression routes.

4.6 Cell and Puzzle Accuracy Decouple Under Compression

A pattern recurs across our compression interventions: cell accuracy and puzzle-exact accuracy decouple. A model can predict most individual cells correctly while satisfying zero global constraints—the signature of a compositional-correctness breakdown that leaves local token prediction intact. We observe it under three distinct interventions:

On knowledge distillation, a single-cycle student (13–15% of teacher parameters) reaches 87.3% (Maze) / 54.8% (Sudoku) cell accuracy but 0.0% puzzle exact (Appendix J, Tables 19 and 20). With structured pruning at 25% sparsity, cell accuracy partially survives (86.4% Maze, 50.0% Sudoku) while puzzle exact is 0.0% on every task. With linear-attention approximation on Maze, replacing softmax attention holds cell accuracy at 87.5% but collapses puzzle exact to 0.0% (Appendix K).

On quantization-aware training, we ran the credible version: training from the calibrated-INT4 Sudoku checkpoint under both cross-entropy and distillation objectives, at three learning rates, with converging training losses (Appendix L). Every configuration degraded held-out accuracy relative to its initialization (Table 21, Appendix L).

Within our training budget, then, a token-level objective does not repair the model it starts from, while per-channel calibration alone lands within 0.3 pp of FP32 on all three tasks (Tables 1 and 3). A shorter-budget run reproduces the same split: high cell accuracy, zero puzzle exact. We do not claim a token-level objective cannot recover reasoning at a larger budget; we claim it is not needed.

The common cause of the decoupling is the objective: cross-entropy and token-distillation losses reward each cell independently, so a model that emits plausible cells without satisfying the puzzle is scored identically to one that solves it. This is not specific to TRM—it applies to any structured-prediction setting where correctness is compositional. Our contribution stands on the post-training side: per-channel calibration recovers Sudoku with no retraining at all (§4.4). What survives compression and what repairs it together fix the configuration worth deploying.

4.7 Optimal Deployment Configuration

The deployment configurations are summarized in Table 7. We measure step latencies, puzzle latencies, and peak memory directly on physical hardware (Samsung Galaxy S24, Samsung Galaxy S22 5G, and Dragonwing RB3 Gen 2) via Qualcomm AI Hub (Table 6). No INT4 configuration was run on device: Table 6 reports FP32 and INT8 latency only, so the 3.26 MB INT4 configuration is a weights-only estimate throughout. INT8 with single-puzzle flash loading and reduced recursion (H=1H{=}1, nsup=8n_{\text{sup}}{=}8) occupies 6.51 MB of weights (analytical) and runs at ∼\sim500 GFLOPs per ARC-AGI-1 puzzle. Weights alone are not the whole footprint: including activations and carry state, the ARC/Maze INT8 streaming peak is 9.51 MB against Sudoku’s 3.06 MB (Table 5, Appendix A), so only Sudoku currently runs inside an 8 MB envelope, and the 4 MB target remains a weights-only projection.

Memory accounting.

Weights alone, weights plus activations, the on-disk artifact and host-process RSS are different quantities. Table 4 gives the scope and provenance of each figure we report.

Maze-Hard is the cleanest deployable case: with no test-time augmentation and no embedding table, its per-pass latency is its per-puzzle latency, and naïve INT4 costs it 0.4 pp (Table 8).

Per-channel calibrated INT4 weights fit under the 4 MB MCU budget (3.26 MB, weights only) and calibration recovers near-FP32 accuracy with no retraining, demonstrated directly on Sudoku-Extreme and, on the official checkpoint, on ARC-AGI-1 (29.4% vs. 29.5% FP32, Table 3; §4.4). The practical compression floor is therefore calibrated INT4, not INT8; naïve INT4 remains unusable, and the fidelity diagnostic separates the two before deployment. The 6×6\times FLOPs reduction also lowers modeled energy proportionally (∼\sim3,000 to ∼\sim500 mJ/puzzle, analytical; Appendix M), and there is no cheaper shortcut through the input: truncating the context destroys accuracy on every task—halving it collapses Maze and Sudoku to 0% puzzle exact (Appendix N).

5 Discussion

Why the architecture split exists.

The two mixers spread their weights differently. Attention encodes sparse relational updates that tolerate coarse noise, whereas MLP-mixing encodes denser token-mixing whose wider per-channel ranges need per-channel scales to survive (Figure 4). Architecture choice in recursive models is therefore a deployment decision, best made at design time.

The microcontroller tier.

We target a regime with kB-to-MB SRAM and no DRAM, where nothing reasoning-capable is deployed today. Mobile-NPU deployment of 1–7B-parameter LLMs is a complementary industrial problem with gigabytes of DRAM to work with, and a 3–7 MB recursive reasoner would be a first entry at our tier. This study establishes the compression recipe that gets a reasoner to that size with its reasoning intact (§3); the streaming peaks fit an 8 MB envelope only on Sudoku (Table 4).

Fidelity should generalize beyond TRM.

Because carry-trajectory fidelity needs only a full-precision reference and the model’s own hidden states (no labels, no task run) it should transfer to any iterative-latent system with accessible state: Universal Transformers (Dehghani et al., 2019), deep equilibrium models, and state-space models.

Limitations

Our study centers on the TRM family across three tasks, with a second architecture (HRM) evaluated only on Sudoku-Extreme; broader generalization across architectures and tasks is untested. The calibrated-INT4 recovery is measured by full-system accuracy on Sudoku and, on the official checkpoint, on ARC (Table 3); the Sudoku TRM-MLP checkpoint is a community reproduction, so its absolute accuracies are not comparable to the original release (App. O). The fidelity diagnostic requires a full-precision reference, so it supports a pre-deployment decision rather than monitoring a live model. ARC accuracies are reported single-pass (no test-time augmentation); TRM’s published protocol uses 1,000-augmentation voting, which would raise both accuracy and per-puzzle deployment cost proportionally. Maze and Sudoku need no augmentation and are the configurations whose latency is directly deployable. One boundary on the claim: every model here is recursive, so the results isolate what recursion does under compression but do not separate that from what being a few-million-parameter model does. A same-size autoregressive control would separate them, and no such checkpoint exists for these tasks.

Appendix A Peak SRAM Memory Footprints

For on-device edge deployment, we evaluate the peak memory footprint under two execution scenarios: a Full Load scenario (where the entire backbone and intermediate activations/carries are stored in SRAM) and a Streaming scenario (where only the current recursive step is loaded, leveraging single-puzzle flash loading of embedding tables).

Table 5 compiles these peak SRAM requirements against a theoretical 8 MB SRAM hardware budget limit.

Under streaming execution, only the Sudoku (INT8) model fits within the 8 MB SRAM budget (3.06 MB streaming peak); the ARC and Maze INT8 models peak at 9.51 MB and so exceed it (§4.7).

Appendix B On-Device Hardware Benchmarks

We compile on-device step and puzzle latencies, peak memory usage, and file sizes directly on three physical edge devices:

  • •

    Samsung Galaxy S24: Featuring the flagship Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 chipset (SM8650, Hexagon v75 NPU).

  • •

    Samsung Galaxy S22 5G: Featuring the Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Gen 1 chipset (SM8450, Hexagon v70 NPU).

  • •

    Dragonwing RB3 Gen 2: Featuring the Qualcomm QCS6490 chipset (Hexagon NPU).

Evaluations are compiled and run via Qualcomm AI Hub targeting native hardware execution. Table 6 reports the full set of consolidated benchmark results.

Static INT8 quantization delivers substantial latency gains for compute-bound tasks with long sequences (ARC-AGI-1 and Maze-Hard) but incurs a step-latency penalty on the computationally light Sudoku-Extreme task, which is dominated instead by NPU driver and dispatch overhead and format-conversion casting; §B.1 works through why.

The controlled quantity is the per-step latency, which is depth-independent by construction: on ARC the FP32→\toINT8 per-step ratio is 40.20→25.6940.20{\to}25.69 ms (1.56×\times). The FP32 and INT8 rows for ARC and Maze run at different recursion depths (H=3H{=}3, nsup=16n_{\text{sup}}{=}16 against H=1H{=}1, nsup=8n_{\text{sup}}{=}8; the depth columns make this explicit), so their per-puzzle ratio combines precision with depth. The Sudoku rows are depth-matched end to end (both H=3H{=}3, nsup=16n_{\text{sup}}{=}16), and there INT8 is slower; §B.1 explains why.

Notebook and on-device harnesses.

The on-device INT8 run scores 26.0% for the H=1H{=}1, nsup=8n_{\text{sup}}{=}8 ARC configuration against 35.25% in the notebook harness, both single-pass. The quantizer accounts for the gap. At FP32 the two harnesses agree to 0.5 pp (35.5% on device, 36.0% in harness); they diverge by 9.3 pp only once INT8 is applied, where bitsandbytes and static QDQ differ. Attributing the residual gap to a specific implementation detail of one quantizer is left to future work.

B.1 Sequence-Length Dependent Quantization Penalty

All rows in Table 6 were compiled through the Qualcomm AI Hub QNN execution provider (libQnnHtp.so) targeting the Hexagon processor; no row falls back to CPU execution. Compilation used enable_htp_fp16_precision=1, so graphs labeled “FP32” execute in FP16 on the Hexagon vector engine (HVX), while INT8 graphs execute on the HTP tensor units with quantize/dequantize (QDQ) boundaries at node interfaces.

The benchmark reveals a counter-intuitive result: while static INT8 quantization accelerates the ARC-AGI-1 and Maze-Hard models, it actually leads to a latency slowdown for the Sudoku-Extreme model per step (from 11.38 ms to 27.23 ms on the S24). This behaviour is a classic small-matrix INT8 penalty governed by the sequence length (TT):

  • •

    Compute-Bound Regime (ARC & Maze): ARC and Maze operate on a sequence length T=900T=900. At this scale, the weight projection matrices are large (900×512900\times 512 by 512×2048512\times 2048), which translates to heavy arithmetic compute (∼\sim187 GFLOPs/step). Moving this workload from the HVX FP16 pipeline to the HTP’s INT8 tensor units reduces execution time significantly, easily overriding the fixed dispatch and QDQ overhead.

  • •

    Overhead-Bound Regime (Sudoku): Sudoku has a sequence length of only T=81T=81 (9797 with padding and embeddings). The matrix multiplications are tiny (e.g., 97×51297\times 512 by 512×2048512\times 2048), requiring only ∼\sim25 MFLOPs/step (7,500×\times less compute than Maze). A 97×51297\times 512 matrix multiplication requires only ∼\sim100K multiply-accumulates, which is too small to saturate the INT8 parallel execution blocks. Consequently, the fixed overhead of the Quantize/Dequantize (QDQ) operators—which convert tensors back and forth at every node boundary—dominates the execution time. While the FP16-on-HVX model runs in a single, unbroken compiler-fused pipeline in 11.38 ms, the INT8 model is penalized by a constant ∼\sim25 ms invocation and marshalling overhead.

Sudoku also relies on token-mixing MLP layers (mlp_t layers of 388 KB/194 KB). These represent extremely small matrices. The Qualcomm Hexagon tensor processor has a minimum efficient tile size threshold; matrix dimensions below this limit fail to trigger accelerated execution paths and fall back to slower scalar execution, further exacerbating the INT8 penalty.

The crossover point where static INT8 quantization becomes beneficial for this recursive transformer architecture on mobile chipsets is approximately T≈200​–​300T\approx 200\text{--}300. Below this threshold, FP16-on-HVX execution remains faster.

B.2 Static vs. Dynamic Quantization

Dynamic quantization preserves full-precision accuracy on every task. Static quantization does not, and Sudoku-Extreme recovers only under selective operator exclusion: leaving activation and carry-state updates in FP32 and quantizing only the MatMul/Gemm weights. The trade-off matters for deployment: dynamic quantization is the robust out-of-the-box path for recursive models, but NPU accelerators require static, pre-allocated tensor boundaries, so on-device execution inherits the static path and its operator exclusions (§B.1). We report this trade-off qualitatively; per-task accuracy under the static path was not separately measured.

Appendix H Architecture Ablation: MLP-Mixing vs. Attention

To separate architecture from task precision we evaluate three recursive architectures on the same task (Sudoku-Extreme) under an identical harness (N=256N{=}256, 16 ACT steps, no TTA; Table 15). TRM-MLP-Mixing and TRM-Attention are the same model family at the same full-precision accuracy (73.873.8 vs. 73.173.1% puzzle exact), differing only in the token mixer; HRM (Wang et al., 2025) is a different recursive architecture (separate high- and low-level modules, attention-based). Under naïve INT4, TRM-MLP-Mixing collapses to 10.210.2% while both attention architectures retain their accuracy. Since TRM-Attention matches TRM-MLP at full precision, this is not an accuracy-headroom effect—the INT4 fragility is specific to MLP-mixing, not the task. The carry-trajectory fidelity diagnostic grades all three correctly (0.350.35 / 0.870.87 / 0.980.98), confirming it generalizes across recursive architectures.

Appendix I Carry-State Diagnostic: Full Data

We measure two carry-state quantities, computed by hooking the shared reasoning module across all recursive calls within one inference pass. Both are computed on real test puzzles (Maze N=64N{=}64, ARC N=32N{=}32, Sudoku N=256N{=}256); the ARC and Maze checkpoints are the public TRM releases, the Sudoku TRM-MLP checkpoint is a community reproduction (see checkpoint provenance, §O), and all numbers below are reproduced from those checkpoints.

Consecutive carry similarity (single-model).

The mean cosine similarity between consecutive carry states (Table 16) is task-specific but insensitive to compression: it is essentially identical under FP32, INT8, and INT4 on every task (changes ≤0.064\leq 0.064), and is therefore a weak failure signal. We report it for completeness; the diagnostic below is the one we recommend.

Carry-trajectory fidelity (vs. full-precision reference).

The recommended diagnostic is the cosine similarity between the quantized model’s final carry state and the FP32 model’s final carry state on the same input—how far quantization pushes the reasoning trajectory off the full-precision path (Table 17). It requires only the FP32 reference (available before deployment) and no task labels. Unlike the consecutive signal, fidelity is graded and monotonic with severity: it stays ≈\approx1.0 wherever INT4 is harmless (Maze, all INT8) and falls in proportion to the accuracy damage—moderately on ARC (0.690.69, −10-10 pp) and catastrophically on Sudoku (0.350.35, −64-64 pp). Per-channel calibrated INT4 recovers fidelity in lockstep with accuracy, so the diagnostic predicts both failure and recovery.

Calibrated INT4 recovers Sudoku.

Measured under an identical evaluation harness (N=256N{=}256, 16 ACT steps, no TTA), naïve per-tensor INT4 collapses Sudoku to 10.210.2% puzzle-exact while per-channel calibrated INT4 recovers to 71.971.9% (vs. 73.873.8% FP32 under the same harness)—i.e., the catastrophic INT4 result is specific to naïve quantization, and the 4 MB MCU target is reachable with calibration (Table 18).

Appendix J Structured Pruning and Knowledge Distillation

Structured pruning.

Magnitude-based structured pruning was evaluated at 25% and 50% sparsity targets across all three tasks (Table 19).

Knowledge distillation.

Student models (hidden=256, 1 layer, 1-cycle) were trained via KL-divergence distillation from the full teacher (Table 20).

Appendix K Linear-Attention Approximation (Maze)

Replacing softmax attention with ELU feature-map linear attention (𝒪⁡(n)\mathcal{O}(n) vs. 𝒪⁡(n2)\mathcal{O}(n^{2})) on Maze illustrates the same cell-vs-puzzle split as quantization: the swap preserves token-level accuracy but destroys puzzle-level reasoning. Evaluated at H=3H{=}3, nsup=1n_{\text{sup}}{=}1 (hence the 78.50% baseline rather than the full-depth 86.80%): zero-shot, cell accuracy holds at 87.3% while puzzle-exact falls to 0.00% (from 78.50% / 99.40%); brief retraining (200 steps) recovers cell accuracy (87.5%) but not puzzle-exact (0.00%). This is a third intervention—alongside pruning and distillation—under which local prediction survives while global constraint satisfaction collapses. Sudoku-Extreme (MLP-mixing) has no attention layers and is not applicable.

Appendix L QAT Configurations

Table 21 reports the six quantization-aware-training configurations of §4.6: two objectives at three learning rates each, 1,000 steps at batch 32 from the calibrated-INT4 initialization (72.3% at step 0).

Appendix M Energy per Inference

Estimated energy follows the FLOPs counts under a Cortex-M55 power model (∼\sim1 mJ/GFLOP): ARC-AGI-1 at full depth (∼\sim3,000 GFLOPs/puzzle) draws ∼\sim3,000 mJ/puzzle, versus ∼\sim500 mJ at the reduced configuration (H=1H{=}1, nsup=8n_{\text{sup}}{=}8). Sudoku-Extreme (∼\sim256 GFLOPs at default depth) draws ∼\sim256 mJ/puzzle. These are analytical estimates under the same FLOPs-based model. The model is precision-blind—it assigns no separate energy-per-operation term to FP32 vs. INT8—so the 6×6\times energy saving follows entirely from the 6×6\times FLOPs (cycle) reduction, not from quantization.

Appendix N Context-Length Truncation

Because attention cost scales as 𝒪⁡(T2)\mathcal{O}(T^{2}), we tested zero-padding the input beyond a truncated context. Truncation is destructive on every task (Table 22): halving the sequence length takes Maze and Sudoku to zero and costs ARC nearly ten points. There is no cheap context shortcut—the full window is load-bearing.

Appendix O Implementation Details

Checkpoint provenance.

The Sudoku TRM-MLP checkpoint is the alphaXiv community reproduction of TRM, whose model card reports 79.37% puzzle exact vs. 87.4% in the original paper. Our Sudoku claims are therefore relative comparisons between compression variants evaluated at matched checkpoints, not absolute-accuracy claims against the original release.

Quantization.

INT8 and INT4 PTQ were applied using bitsandbytes v0.41 (Dettmers et al., 2022) with load_in_8bit=True and load_in_4bit=True respectively. Per-channel calibration for INT4 calibrated used 128 calibration puzzles drawn from the training set.

Carry-state extraction.

shs_{h} was computed by registering a forward hook on the carry-state update function gϕg_{\phi} to capture ZhZ_{h} at each outer cycle. Cosine similarity was computed token-wise and averaged across the sequence dimension and across all puzzles in the evaluation set.

QAT.

The headline QAT runs (§4.6) initialize from the calibrated-INT4 checkpoint and fine-tune for 1,000 steps at batch 32, under cross-entropy and token-distillation objectives at learning rates 10−510^{-5}, 10−410^{-4}, and 10−310^{-3}, with the deep-supervision ACT loop. A shorter probe (100 steps, lr=10−5\text{lr}{=}10^{-5}, cross-entropy, batch 4, from the naïve INT4 checkpoint) is the held-out run cited in §4.6. Training and evaluation used the Modal cloud platform.

ONNX export and edge deployment.

Models were exported to ONNX format using torch.onnx.export for deployment via ONNX Runtime and Qualcomm AI Hub. The ONNX export produces a single-step model (TRMBackboneStep) that executes one H-cycle step, with the outer recursion loop managed by the inference harness.
